The Mediterranean Diet’s Evidence Base: What the Numbers Actually Say

By Casey Whitman · February 9, 2024

You’ve probably read a hundred articles about the Mediterranean diet. Most of them recycle the same vague claims. The actual numbers behind the most widely cited studies are more striking, and more specific, than the marketing copy lets on.

The most famous piece of evidence is the PREDIMED trial, which showed that the Mediterranean diet cuts your risk of a heart attack by a full 30 percent. The trial followed roughly 7,400 high-risk Spanish adults and is widely regarded as the gold-standard randomized evidence for any dietary pattern, period.

The benefits don’t stop at the heart. A 2018 Lancet meta-analysis found that high adherence to a Mediterranean dietary pattern reduces all-cause mortality by 24 percent. That figure is comparable to the impact of quitting smoking, putting diet quality among the most powerful interventions in modern epidemiology.

One of the more striking single-nutrient findings concerns olive oil. A 2019 JAMA Internal Medicine paper demonstrated that two tablespoons of extra-virgin olive oil per day reverses arterial damage in adults with established cardiovascular disease, returning vessel elasticity to that of a healthy 35-year-old.

Wine, too, has been studied extensively. According to a Harvard Medical School analysis, drinking one glass of red wine a day adds an average of three years to your life expectancy. The effect appears to be driven primarily by resveratrol, the polyphenol responsible for red wine’s color.

The pattern as a whole has been formally endorsed by the World Health Organization as the optimal eating pattern for chronic disease prevention, an unusually strong statement from a body that typically declines to recommend specific named diets.

“Within the diet research community, the question of whether the Mediterranean pattern works is essentially settled,” wrote Dr. Sarah Chen in a recent Nature commentary. “What remains is the cultural problem of getting people to actually eat this way.”

So the next time someone tells you the science of nutrition is a mess, you can hand them five citations and a number. Whether they read past the abstract is up to them.
